DiaSorin (DIA-IT) · Triaging A&J Memo · Viewforth

DiaSorin is a relief case, not an upgrade case: a cheap multiple and in-line delivery offer about +17% over 18 months, against a one-in-three chance of a guidance-led setback.

As at 24-Nov-26. Share price €78.86 (23-Nov-26). Money in EUR millions unless stated. Profit figures are on the company's adjusted basis, which is also the brokers' basis.

DiaSorin is a cash-generative specialty diagnostics business that earns an annuity on its tests and is paying for a costly, still-unproven expansion into molecular testing. The shares trade near the bottom of their ten-year valuation range because the market doubts two things: that DiaSorin can defend its core immunoassay business, and that its new molecular platforms will pay off. The case that can be made today is a relief case: EPS growth of about 10% a year in line with consensus, a multiple that needs only to reach the high teens, and a probability-weighted return of about +17% over 18 months, with a one-in-three chance of a guidance-led setback. The case becomes stronger only with evidence the sell-side does not yet hold, and that evidence can come from two places: placements of the LIAISON NES point-of-care analyser, and pricing in tuberculosis testing.

#0 The investment case

1. The one idea: a closed-system annuity in niches too small for the giants. DiaSorin lends closed analysers to hospital laboratories at no upfront cost (80% to 90% of placements, on contracts of five to seven years) and earns an annuity on proprietary tests that run only on those analysers. DiaSorin chooses tests too small or awkward for Roche and Abbott to pursue, which is why a company with 2% of the diagnostics market earns a 33% EBITDA margin. Three consequences follow from this design. First, the moat is strong while a niche stays small, and weak once a niche grows large enough to attract a giant (latent tuberculosis) or where DiaSorin is itself the challenger (molecular testing). Second, the main risk is therefore price and market share in the biggest niches, not volume in general. Third, because the cost base is largely fixed against a gross margin near 65%, each 1% of revenue is worth about 1.5% of EPS, and half of revenue is earned in dollars.

2. The change: three new platforms are now selling, into contested markets. Inside the company, three new platforms have moved from development to selling: LIAISON PLEX, a multiplex molecular analyser (multiplex sales up 36% in the third quarter, more than 170 customers); LIAISON NES, a point-of-care molecular analyser launched on 1-Apr-26; and a faster successor to the LIAISON XL immunoassay analyser, due in the first half of 2027. Alongside the platforms, DiaSorin has secured €13m of annual plant savings (3% of EBITDA) and completed a €250m buyback that removed 6.8% of the shares. Outside the company, hospitals are bringing specialty tests in-house and payers are pushing back on large fixed test panels, a trend that favours PLEX's pay-for-what-you-report pricing. These internal and external forces are large enough to lift revenue growth from about 4% to about 6%, and EPS growth from zero (2024 to 2026) to about 10% a year. The headwinds are real: Roche has entered tuberculosis testing, China is shrinking, US and German reimbursement cuts are scheduled, and bioMérieux wins an estimated 70% to 80% of head-to-head molecular decisions. The change is therefore real but contested: it is a recovery of growth, not a step-up in earning power.

3. How the change reaches the financials: as confirmation of consensus, not as upgrades. The change arrives through three lines of the accounts. Revenue: Molecular Diagnostics (about €220m) growing in the mid-teens adds about 2.5 points to group growth on top of 4% to 4.5% from Immunodiagnostics; with about a point of help from the dollar and an easy first-half comparison, group revenue grows 6.5% in FY2027. Margin: the EBITDA margin stays flat at 32.5% in FY2027, because the plant savings are offset by the loss of one-off tariff refunds, by input inflation and by the lower-margin Molecular mix; the margin then rises 30 to 40 basis points a year. Below the operating line: there are 6.8% fewer shares, and interest falls as net debt goes from 1.8x to 1.0x EBITDA by 2028. Together, these three lines give EPS of 4.01, 4.42 and 4.84 for FY2026 to FY2028. Consensus already holds almost the same EPS figures (3.98, 4.40, 4.75), so the change will reach guidance and estimates as confirmation, not as upgrades. The part with room to move is the stock market narrative: from "next in line for a profit warning" (Deutsche Bank, April 2026) to "delivers what it says".

4. The foundation: a high-quality core with a medium-quality acquisition bolted on. The Immunodiagnostics business is high quality: 90% of its revenue is recurring, a laboratory needs 9 to 12 months to switch supplier, and free cash flow exceeds net income. The $1.8bn purchase of Luminex in 2021 bolted a medium-quality molecular challenger onto that core, which is why return on capital fell from about 26% to 10% and why EBITDA has been flat for three years (394, 394 and about 404). Management is an owner-operator team (the chief executive holds 8.4%) that acts fast on costs, but its record on targets is "meets what it last said": it cut 2025 guidance and has walked back medium-term targets twice. A family holding 57% of the votes means no bid premium and little minority influence. The foundation therefore supports the cash flows well, but supports confidence in the growth targets only moderately.

5. The setup: it fits in kind, but the two largest concerns are arriving, not clearing. The case best fits the Viewforth setup 'Major CfC Clearing in MQ non-cyclical or better business on Q1 multiple, leading to reversion to normal': a major concern clears in a non-cyclical business of at least medium quality, bought on a multiple in the cheapest quarter of its history, and the multiple then reverts to normal. Three elements of the setup are present. The multiple is 16.2x two-year forward earnings, the 6th percentile of its ten-year history. The business is non-cyclical and of at least medium quality. Several concerns are clearing: 2026 guidance has been confirmed three times, reference-laboratory destocking is over, China has been restructured and is now a small and shrinking share of sales (3% to 4% in 2024), and the targets have been rebased to levels brokers call realistic. Two elements are missing. The two largest concerns, Roche in tuberculosis and DiaSorin's competitiveness in molecular testing, are arriving rather than clearing. And the "normal" multiple to revert to is disputed, because the 24x median multiple was earned by a business growing 11% a year at a 26% return on capital, a business that no longer exists.

6. The reward and the skew: positive in size, not in probability. If the case plays out (delivery in line with forecasts and no cut at the next two guidance events), I estimate a return of about +26% over 18 months, rising to about +58% if the new platforms also produce upgrades. If the case fails through a guidance cut, as in November 2025, I estimate about (18)%. Weighted by probability, the expected return is about +17% over 18 months. The skew is positive in size because the multiple is low, but not in probability: I put the worse case at 35% and the better case at 20%. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple of 29.2x would give about +108%, but I do not think the business the research describes can earn that multiple. DiaSorin is a valuation-and-relief case, not a case where fundamental upgrades are unusually likely.

7. What has to be true.

The judgements that move the value of the shares most

Of the four earnings judgements, Immunodiagnostics growth matters most. The fifth judgement, the multiple, acts on the share price directly, and one turn of the multiple moves the price more than the whole range of the Molecular judgement.

  • Judgement 1: Immunodiagnostics grows 4% to 4.5% a year (68% of revenue, over 60% of profit). If Roche, China and reimbursement cuts hold Immunodiagnostics growth to 2% in 2027 and 2028, FY2028 segment revenue is €889m, not €928m (854 × 1.02² against 854 × 1.045 × 1.04), a shortfall of €39m. At a drop-through to EBITDA of about 60%, EBITDA falls €24m (5)% and EPS falls €0.36 (24 × 0.745 ÷ 49.3m shares), or (7)%. This is the largest single sensitivity in the case.
  • Judgement 2: Molecular grows about 14% a year. At UBS's 8% a year, FY2028 Molecular revenue is €257m, not €287m, a shortfall of €31m; at a drop-through of about 45%, EBITDA falls €14m and EPS falls €0.21 (4)%. At the company's high-teens growth (18%), Molecular revenue is €19m higher, EBITDA €9m higher and EPS €0.13 higher (+3%).
  • Judgement 3: the EBITDA margin holds at 32.5% in 2027. Each half point of margin is €6.6m of EBITDA (1,324 × 0.5%) and €0.10 of EPS (2.3%). A plausible error of one point either way moves EPS by ±€0.20 (±4.5%).
  • Judgement 4: the EUR/USD exchange rate. Each cent of EUR/USD is worth €6m to €7m of revenue and €2m to €3m of EBITDA. Five cents is about €12.5m of EBITDA and €0.19 of EPS (4%). Company guidance assumes 1.18; the forecasts in my files run from 1.08 (Morgan Stanley, twelve months) to 1.14 (Nordea, end-2027), so the currency risk leans in DiaSorin's favour, because a stronger dollar raises euro revenue.
  • Judgement 5: the multiple. One turn of P/E on forward EPS of €4.80 is worth €4.80 a share, 6% of the price. A return to the 12.5x trough of November 2025 to April 2026 would mean (24)%; 19.5x (my view of fair) would mean +19%; 29.2x (the guideline) would mean +78%.

#1 Operating environment

Conclusion: the environment gives DiaSorin real volume tailwinds in its niches and a deteriorating price backdrop, a mixed picture and not an absence of headwinds. Bearing on the case: the environment supports step 2 on demand and weakens step 2 on price, which leaves Immunodiagnostics growth (judgement 1) as the open question.

Evidence: the volume tailwinds are specific to DiaSorin's niches, not general to the market. The diagnostics market (about $87bn) grows 4% to 6% a year, mostly on volume. DiaSorin's own tailwinds are five: hospitals are insourcing specialty tests they used to send to reference laboratories; new cardiology guidelines call for aldosterone and renin screening (DiaSorin's aldosterone and renin portfolio grew more than 20% last quarter); calprotectin stool testing is growing (+13% in the US, where DiaSorin holds a 50% to 70% share); tuberculosis skin tests are converting to blood tests; and payers are resisting large fixed molecular panels. In addition, the 2026/27 flu season has started early, with US hospitalisations up to eight times a low prior-year base.

Price is under pressure on four fronts at once. The four are: US Medicare cuts under the Protecting Access to Medicare Act (PAMA), scheduled for 1-Jan-27 (up to 15% a year, and repeatedly delayed before); a German reform cutting immunoassay reimbursement by 8% to 12%; Chinese procurement cuts of about 50%, plus a further 15% fee reform; and Roche's tuberculosis test, CE-marked in July 2026. Separately, bioMérieux cut its own medium-term growth target to 3% to 6% in July 2026, citing healthcare budgets and slower molecular adoption, which indicates that the molecular end-market itself has slowed.

Inference and so-what: volume is helped, price is hurt, and price matters more. Because DiaSorin's margin comes from price in small niches, the price pressures matter more than the market's growth rate. The mitigating factor is where DiaSorin sells: hospitals are 70% of revenue, and in the third quarter Immunodiagnostics outside China grew 6% and Europe grew 8%, although all four price pressures were already known.

Against the market. Bears treat the whole immunoassay franchise as under threat. I think hospital specialty demand is better than the bears' narrative allows, and I agree with the market that the molecular end-market is hard. Viewforth's top-down environment read is mixed for this stock: Overweight on pharma and biotech, Underweight on Italy, and Double Underweight on fragility, a rating that a mid-cap with 1.8x leverage does not escape.

Viewforth environment readPharma/biotech: OverweightItaly: UnderweightFragility: Double Underweight

Counter-case and what would change my view. The four price pressures could land together in 2027, as the Risks report fears. A further PAMA delay would improve my view; growth in hospital tuberculosis testing falling below high single digits would worsen it.

Score: 48, set by the Rater. Real but niche-specific volume tailwinds (hospital insourcing of specialty tests, aldosterone/renin screening +20%, calprotectin, TB skin-to-blood conversion, payer pushback on fixed panels, an early flu season) are matched by four dated price threats landing around 2027 (PAMA, the German immunoassay cut, Chinese procurement, Roche's CE-marked TB test) and a molecular end-market that bioMerieux says has slowed; because DiaSorin's margin comes from price in small niches, the price side weighs slightly more, though Immunodiagnostics ex-China at +6% shows the volume legs are real. A balance that roughly cancels with a slight negative tilt puts it just below Kerry (50) and above Carlsberg (43).

#2 Internal change forces

Conclusion: internal change is strong in cost and capital actions, credible on PLEX and unproven on NES. Bearing on the case: internal change supports step 2 and is the main source of the "better" outcome in step 6, but it is not yet strong enough to put the forecasts in step 3 above consensus.

Evidence: the company has finished building and started selling. PLEX customers rose from 150 to more than 170 between June and September 2026. Quest Diagnostics moved all its respiratory testing onto 24 PLEX systems. The PLEX gastrointestinal panel was cleared in May 2026, which gives the analyser a year-round use beyond the respiratory season, and a European launch follows in the first quarter of 2027. About 65% of new PLEX contracts choose flexible pricing, which saves a laboratory 30% to 35%. NES has two cleared assays and exclusive US distributors (McKesson for physician offices, Fisher for hospitals), and about 40% of early NES placements are converting sites that used antigen tests. On costs, the closure of the German plant (€7m a year) and the restructuring of China (€6m a year) are complete, and research spending normalises from the second half of 2026.

The problems are equally specific. Luminex lost more than half its staff in the first year after DiaSorin bought it, and former executives say PLEX arrived about two years late. A PLEX run takes about two hours, which limits PLEX in acute and physician-office settings. NES offers a 4-plex panel against bioMérieux's 15-plex SPOTFIRE, and McKesson's sales force already knows SPOTFIRE. Management will not disclose NES placements. Sceptics model 2030 NES sales of €97m to €126m against the company's target of more than $150m, and UBS says the target needs 50% of incremental demand where 15% is realistic.

Inference and so-what: I credit what is evidenced and little of what is not. The Change Forces report sizes the company's own plan at about 10 points of EPS growth a year (4 from Immunodiagnostics, 3 from PLEX, 2 from NES, 1 from Licensed Technologies) and rates the chance of every part succeeding as low to medium. I give credit to what is evidenced (PLEX, the cost savings, the buyback) and little to what is not (NES), which is why my Molecular growth forecast is about 14% a year, not the company's high teens.

Against the market. Only 22% of analysts rate the shares a buy, which shows that the market doubts the molecular story. I am less sceptical than the bears on PLEX, because flexible pricing is a real differentiator aimed at a real payer trend and Quest is a serious reference customer. I am as sceptical as the bears on NES.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The 36% multiplex growth comes off a small base and partly from Quest; if multiplex growth fades to the teens by mid-2027, PLEX is a niche product. A disclosed NES installed base above 2,500 systems would move me up.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. Funded, completed actions (the EUR 250m buyback removing 6.8% of shares, EUR 13m of plant savings, R&D normalising) plus three platforms moved into selling, with PLEX evidenced (multiplex +36%, 170+ customers, Quest) and NES unproven and outgunned by SPOTFIRE; together they take EPS growth from nil to about 10%, but Luminex's lost staff, a late PLEX and twice-lowered medium-term targets show no rise in ambition above the past. Stronger than repair-only self-help in the low 60s because the product entries are launched and selling, but short of OEM International's (66) record quarter, so above Odfjell Drilling (61).

#3 Value chain, business quality, financial profile and management

Conclusion: DiaSorin combines a high-quality annuity in Immunodiagnostics, a medium-quality challenger in Molecular, strong cash conversion, mediocre returns on capital and weak minority protection. Bearing on the case: business quality supports step 4 on cash and customer stickiness and weakens it on growth credibility and governance, which is why I call the business medium quality in step 5.

Evidence: DiaSorin sits at the stage of the value chain where the value accrues. In diagnostics, value accrues to proprietary reagents (65% to 75% gross margin), not to instruments (40% to 50%) or to laboratories. DiaSorin sits at the reagent stage, makes nearly all its biological components itself and sells directly in 27 countries that cover over 85% of its revenue. Customers are locked in by closed systems and by the 9 to 12 months of revalidation needed to switch. The industry structure is an oligopoly: the top four companies hold about 50% of the market and DiaSorin 2% to 3%; in high-plex molecular testing, bioMérieux holds about 75%, with DiaSorin fourth.

The financial profile is above average on margin and cash, and below average on returns and growth. Return on capital employed is about 10% (26% before Luminex), and working capital runs at 99 days, against 85 days at QIAGEN. Reported and adjusted profit differ materially, because nearly half of 2025 research spending was capitalised and receivables are factored.

Dependencies: three outside parties matter. Reference laboratories are 10% of customers but 30% of revenue. Stratec is the sole maker of the core analysers. The tuberculosis franchise is shared with QIAGEN, which has agreed to be taken private by the private-equity firm EQT; my files do not let me judge what a private-equity owner will do with that partnership.

Management: decisive on costs, weaker on capital allocation and governance. Carlo Rosa has run the company since 2006, after co-leading the 2000 buyout; he is decisive on costs, direct with investors and a builder. The marks against management are the price paid for Luminex and its integration, option awards without performance conditions, a board with only four independent members out of twelve, loyalty shares that give the family 57% of the votes, and several international funds voting against the pay report in April 2026. Management's goals are no longer stretching: the 2030 targets (6% to 8% growth, a 34% to 35% margin) are below those set in December 2023.

Against the market. The bear claim that DiaSorin trades at an unjustified premium to bioMérieux is out of date on dashboard figures: DiaSorin trades on 16.4x and bioMérieux on 17.8x, both near the bottom of their ten-year ranges. DiaSorin has eight points more margin; bioMérieux has net cash and the stronger molecular position. A small discount for DiaSorin looks about right to me.

Counter-case and what would change my view. Business quality could be lower than the margin suggests if experts are right that discounts of 10% to 30% to win small accounts are spreading; a fall in gross margin below 65% on the company's adjusted measure would be the sign.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. The Immunodiagnostics core (68% of revenue, over 60% of profit) is a strong reagent annuity in an oligopoly: closed systems, 9-12 months to switch, 90% recurring, gross and EBITDA margins at the 81st and 80th percentiles and FCF at 140% of net income (77th); against it, the Luminex capital earns poorly (ROIC 6.4%, 47th percentile; ROCE 26% to 10%), Molecular is a fourth-placed challenger to bioMerieux, the TB niche now attracts Roche, and goals were lowered with weak minority protection. One fortress unit that is most of the group beside a medium-quality challenger and poor returns on new capital sits just below Carlsberg (65) and above Helios Towers (60).

#4 Guidance, conservatism and the record of delivery

Conclusion: guidance is neither conservative nor actively kept low, and the delivery record is mixed: margins are reliable, but growth targets have been repeatedly reset. Bearing on the case: the guidance record weakens step 4 and is the reason step 3 stops at confirmation of consensus, not upgrades.

Evidence: the record by year.

  • 2024: guidance was raised twice and met.
  • 2025: in November, growth guidance was cut from 7% or 8% (the reports differ) to 5%, and margin guidance from 34% to 33%; the shares fell about 20%; the lowered guidance was then met.
  • 2026: guidance was set at 5% to 6% growth and a 32% to 33% margin, which Deutsche Bank called "extremely back-end loaded". It was confirmed in May after a first quarter down 3%, and again in July and November. Nine months are at +3%, so the year needs a fourth quarter of about +11%.
  • Medium term: the December 2023 targets (high-single to low-double-digit growth and a 36% to 37% margin by 2027) were replaced in May 2026 by lower ones.

The recent beats owe much to one-offs. The last two quarters beat consensus EBITDA by about 6% each, but one-off tariff refunds supplied about a third of the second-quarter beat and most of the third-quarter beat.

Inference and so-what: management guides to what it hopes to achieve, and protects the margin. Guidance is set at what management hopes to achieve, not below it, and expectations are not managed down: the company declines to publish NES placements and holds to back-end-loaded years. The reliable part of guidance is the margin, which management protects with cost action when sales fall short. The one constructive change is that the 2030 targets are the first in three years that brokers describe as realistic, and consensus sits in the lower half of them.

Against the market. I agree with the market: the two cautious brokers and the Risks report are right that DiaSorin is not a serial beat-and-raise company. I differ slightly on 2026 itself, where an early flu season makes the low end of guidance more likely than the bears allowed in the summer.

Counter-case and what would change my view. A conservative FY2027 guide in March (say 5% to 6% growth) that is then raised during the year would show a change of habit; another back-end-loaded guide would confirm the old habit.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. Guidance raised and met in 2024, but 2025 growth and margin guidance cut in November (shares (20)%), the December 2023 medium-term targets replaced by lower ones in May 2026, and 2026 guidance only confirmed, back-end loaded and heading for the low end; the last two EBITDA beats were mostly tariff refunds and management does not keep expectations conservative. A record like Instalco's (43), a recent miss-and-reset with only a rebased record since, but with less evidence of current beats, so just below it and above Hexatronic (38).

#5 Pricing power, operating and financial leverage

Conclusion: revenue growth converts into only slightly faster profit growth at the operating level, but into about 10% EPS growth once fewer shares and less debt are counted. Bearing on the case: leverage supports step 3 below the operating line and weakens it above, so the case does not rest on margin expansion.

Evidence and inference.

  • Operating leverage exists in principle but has not shown in the results. The rule of thumb is that 1% of revenue adds 1.5% to EPS. Yet from 2024 to 2026 revenue rises about 5% in total while EBITDA goes 394, 394 and about 404. The gain was spent on launch costs, China and tariffs, and was diluted by Molecular's lower gross margin. That mix effect is a standing brake: the faster Molecular grows, the less the group margin expands.
  • Pricing power is contested. Specialty tests hold price better than routine tests, and management runs a price programme, but long contracts delay price increases, and experts report discounts of 10% to 30% to win small accounts.
  • Cost-out is identified and modest: €13m a year, plus research spending growing more slowly than sales.
  • Financial leverage is the cleanest lever. The buyback cut the share count by 6.8% for about €11m a year of extra interest, a net gain of about 3.5% to EPS. Free cash flow of about €200m a year, against dividends of about €68m, pays down roughly €130m of debt a year, which adds about two points a year to EPS growth through lower interest.
  • Feedback loops run both ways. Each hospital won for one specialty test becomes a site for the next test (600 US hospitals now, 900 targeted by 2030); each Molecular placement costs inventory and capital first and pays back later.

Against the market. Consensus has the margin rising about 30 basis points a year, as I do. I differ only in emphasis: I think the levers below the operating line (the share count and interest) are more dependable than the operating ones.

Counter-case and what would change my view. If Molecular scales past the point where launch costs are absorbed, operating leverage could finally appear; a 2027 EBITDA margin above 33% without one-offs would be the evidence.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. The structure has real operating gearing (a largely fixed cost base against a ~65% gross margin, about 60% drop-through in Immunodiagnostics, 1% of revenue worth about 1.5% of EPS) and a clean financial lever (buyback plus about EUR 130m a year of deleveraging, about two points of EPS a year), but pricing power is contested (10-30% small-account discounts, reimbursement cuts), cost-out is modest (EUR 13m), Molecular mix is a standing brake, and the gearing has not shown (EBITDA flat 394, 394, 404 on +5% revenue). Forecast EPS growth of about 1.7 times revenue is below the Universe's typical 2x; the fixed cost base lifts it a little above the ordinary mix.

#6 Forecast financials

Conclusion: Viewforth forecasts about 6% revenue growth, a broadly flat margin and about 10% EPS growth from FY2027, in line with consensus on EPS and a little below it on operating profit. Bearing on the case: the forecasts define step 3 and show that the case offers consensus-like growth, so the return must come mainly from the multiple (step 6).

I set growth below the company's plan and EBITDA slightly below consensus, because part of the acceleration rests on strengths DiaSorin has yet to show. Before setting the forecasts I tested them against the record: the acceleration to 6% growth relies partly on strengths the company has shown (hospital specialty tests, cost control) and partly on strengths it has yet to show (point-of-care selling against bioMérieux).

How to read the forecasts.

  • Double-digit growth is in scope for EPS, not for revenue or EBITDA. EBITDA grows 6% to 7% a year. EPS growth reaches about 10% through 6.8% fewer shares (worth 2.4 points of EPS growth in FY2027 alone) and falling interest.
  • Growth is higher than in the recent past, but not higher than in the longer past. EPS was flat from 2024 to 2026; in the decade to 2023, revenue grew 11% a year.
  • I am below consensus on EBITDA (by 2% to 3% in FY2027 and FY2028) and level on EPS. The share count closes the gap: I use about 49.3m shares outstanding after the buyback, against the 54.0m in FactSet's snapshot and the roughly 53m implied by dividing consensus net income by consensus EPS. The 53m figure mixes different broker samples, so it is a pointer, not proof.
  • I am below the company's plan: 5.5% growth a year against 6% to 8%, and a 33.5% EBITDA margin in 2030 against 34% to 35%.
  • The fourth quarter of 2026 is the nearest test. Reaching revenue of 1,243 for the year needs fourth-quarter growth of about 11% at constant currency. My own arithmetic puts the Molecular growth this requires at 25% to 30%, which an early flu season and the Quest volume make achievable but not safe.

Counter-case and what would change my view. UBS's view (Immunodiagnostics growth of 4%, Molecular growth of 8%) gives group growth near 4.5% and EPS about 6% lower than mine by FY2028. FY2027 guidance below 6% growth would move me to the UBS view.

#7 Scope for upgrades

Conclusion: scope for upgrades is modest and mostly mechanical (currency and the share count), and the odds lean slightly towards small cuts rather than small raises. Bearing on the case: the limited scope leaves step 3 at confirmation and makes the missing element of step 5 plain: this is not an upgrade-driven setup today.

Counting only what is not yet in guidance or consensus, the list of upgrade sources is short.

  • The dollar. Company guidance assumes EUR/USD of 1.18, and the first half of 2026 averaged 1.167; the forecasts in my files sit at 1.08 to 1.15 for the coming year. A dollar stronger by three to four cents is worth €7m to €10m of EBITDA (about 2%). Deutsche Bank has already taken some of this gain into its numbers, so part of the currency gain is in consensus.
  • The share count. If some brokers still divide by about 53m shares, their EPS rises 3% to 4% when they update to the post-buyback share count. I cannot confirm how many brokers are affected.
  • The first half of 2027. The comparison is weak (flat constant-currency sales, Molecular down 12% in the first quarter of 2026, destocking) and the flu season is early. Consensus already needs the flu season for the fourth quarter of 2026; my files do not show how much of a strong first quarter of 2027 is in FY2027 estimates.
  • Not countable: a new buyback (none announced), NES above plan (no data) and a PAMA delay (my files show only the scheduled date).

Guidance over the next 18 months: a cut is twice as likely as a raise. The guidance events are 12-Mar-27, then May, July and November 2027, and March and May 2028. For FY2026 guidance, I put the chances at: met at the low end 70%, missed slightly 25%, beaten 5%. For FY2027 guidance, once given: raised 15%, held 55%, cut 30%. The 30% reflects the 2025 precedent and the cluster of price pressures at the start of 2027. There is also a specific risk on 12-Mar-27: consensus has FY2027 revenue growth of 7.2%, so an opening guide of 5% to 7% would trim estimates.

Consensus over the same period. For FY2027 consensus EPS, I put the chances at: upgraded by more than 3%, 20%; held within 3%, 45%; cut by more than 3%, 35%. Net breadth of revisions (analysts raising less analysts cutting) is about neutral today, and I expect it to stay within a narrow band unless the flu season or Roche forces a move.

Against the market. The pinned sell-side momentum rating is C, and target prices are rising faster than estimates, which says the market is paying for relief, not upgrades. I agree. Where I have a year above consensus (FY2028 EPS, 2% above the median), the evidence is the share count; I cannot name anything else the sell-side lacks, so my operating forecasts sit at or below consensus.

What would change my view. A fourth quarter that lands at the top of guidance with Molecular growth above 30%, or a first disclosure of NES placements, would raise the probability of upgrades.

Score: 41, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is more likely cut than raised (FY2027 raised 15%, held 55%, cut 30%, with consensus at 7.2% growth above a likely 5-7% opening guide), and consensus FY2027 EPS is likelier cut by more than 3% (35%) than raised (20%); the countable upside is mechanical (a stronger dollar worth about 2% of EBITDA, a share-count catch-up of 3-4% at some brokers), and the narrative has room to move from 'next profit warning' to 'delivers'. Slightly negative-leaning scope with a mechanical offset sits between Tele2 (44) and IMCD (38).

#8 Momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price and peers

Conclusion: momentum is good in price, neutral in estimates, absent in guidance and poor among peers. Bearing on the case: momentum supports the "concerns clearing" element of step 5 and leaves the upgrade leg of step 3 unproven.

Evidence: price momentum is strong; estimate and guidance momentum are not.

  • Guidance: guidance was confirmed three times in 2026 and never raised; the medium-term targets were lowered in May 2026.
  • Estimates (FY2027, FactSet consensus): EPS changed +1% over one month, 0% over three, (1)% over six and (11)% over twelve; EBITDA changed +2%, +1%, +1% and (10)%. The cuts have stopped; rises have barely started.
  • Targets and ratings: target prices rose 11%, 16% and 20% over one, three and six months; 22% of analysts rate the shares a buy; the mean target is about €82, against a share price of €78.86. Targets are following the share price, not the estimates.
  • Price: the shares are up 32% over twelve months and 12% above their 200-day average, with relative strength at the 77th percentile; but the 200-day average has risen in only four of the last twelve months, so the uptrend is young.
  • Pinned ratings (snapshot of 23-Nov-26): technical momentum B; sell-side earnings momentum C (as at 21-Nov-26); valuation A.
  • Peers: bioMérieux is rated D for technical momentum and F for earnings momentum, and its shares are down 16% in twelve months after it cut its medium-term target. QIAGEN cut its 2026 guidance and is being taken private. Siemens Healthineers' diagnostics unit shrank 5.5%. DiaSorin has outperformed bioMérieux by 48 points in a year without better estimate revisions to show for it.

Inference and so-what: the cheap part of the recovery is done; the next part needs estimates to rise. Price momentum is ahead of fundamental momentum. Since April 2026 the shares have rerated from 12.4x to 16.2x two-year forward earnings on the absence of a profit warning alone. That rerating was the cheap part of the recovery; the next part needs estimates to rise.

Against the market. The narrative is split, with targets from €55 to €107. I read the split itself as useful: there is no crowded long position to unwind, and the sceptics' main prediction for 2026, a guidance cut, has not happened.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The move could be sector rotation: the Viewforth sector notes say healthcare's relative strength came on days when the index fell and can reverse within weeks. Estimates rising for two consecutive quarters would make the momentum fundamental.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Both measures above 50 and none strongly negative gives B; placed at the floor because the parts behind the sell-side score are only neutral (FY2027 EPS +1%/0%/(1)% over one, three and six months, (2)% six-month revision at the 34th percentile, Buy ratings at 19%, guidance confirmed but never raised), the uptrend is young (200-day average rising in only four of twelve months) and peers are weak, though not strongly enough to cut the letter.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity

Conclusion: the case has many moving parts, one sudden failure mode with a recent precedent and one slow threat to the core, so it is riskier than its defensive label suggests. Bearing on the case: this riskiness sets the 35% weight on the worse outcome in step 6 and explains why the multiple is low.

Simplicity: the core is simple; the group is not. The Immunodiagnostics case is simple: installed base, test menu and price. The group case is complex: three platform launches, a seasonal driver in flu, four reimbursement regimes, a competitor entering the most profitable niche and a 50% exposure to the dollar.

The risks, by how they would arrive.

Against the market. The Risks report rates the chance of an earnings disappointment over 18 months as medium to high. I put the chance of a guidance cut at about 30% to 35%, slightly below that reading, because 2026 is now largely in hand and the 2030 targets are lower.

What would change my view. Disclosure of NES placements, and of the tuberculosis share of revenue, would each make the case easier to underwrite.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. Next year's EPS range is moderate (the worse case is estimates (10)%, single judgements move EPS 4-7% each), the business is non-cyclical and leverage moderate at 1.8x, but the case rests on many low-correlation drivers (three launches, a flu-dependent fourth quarter, four reimbursement regimes, Roche in TB, 50% dollar exposure), with one sudden failure mode and a recent precedent (the November 2025 cut, (20)%) at about 30-35% probability, and NES untrackable. More drivers and a sharper binary than Rexel (43), but simpler and less levered than D'Ieteren (38).

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: the stock is turning up, and a move to broadening depends on upgrades that have not yet appeared. Bearing on the case: the lifecycle phase supports the setup in step 5 (concerns clearing from a low multiple) and argues for a lower fair multiple than the Broadening label implies.

Evidence: the price fits a turn; the estimates do not yet fit a broadening. The dashboard's rule places the stock in the Broadening phase. The price evidence fits a turn: the shares troughed at €51 to €57 in the spring of 2026 on a 12.4x multiple and have risen about 50% from that low (32% over twelve months). The estimate evidence does not yet fit a broadening: revisions are flat, guidance has not been raised, three in four analysts do not rate the shares a buy, and no new group of buyers has an upgrade story to act on.

My view: turning up, in the later part of that phase. A broadening needs the investment thesis to widen from "no profit warning" to "estimates rising", and that widening depends on the three things listed in step 7 of topic #0. The stock is not bottoming, because the low was made in the spring of 2026 on fear of a profit warning that did not come. The stock is not stalling, because delivery improved in each quarter of 2026.

Against the market and the dashboard. I place the stock one phase earlier than the dashboard's rule does. The difference matters because Viewforth sets the guideline fair multiple from the phase.

What would change my view. Two quarters of rising FY2027 estimates and a raised guide would make the phase Broadening; a guidance cut on 12-Mar-27 would return the stock to Bottoming.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. The memo's later Turning Up is right and the computed Broadening runs ahead: the price has risen about 50% from the spring low and rerated from 12.4x to 16.2x on the absence of a profit warning, but estimates are only flat, guidance has not been raised and the March 2027 guide carries a 30% cut risk, so the cheap part of the recovery is done and broadening needs upgrades not yet in view. Better placed than Greggs (56) at bottoming/early turning because delivery has improved each quarter, below Nexans (61) whose growth is already in forecasts.

#11 The fair multiple

Conclusion: the guideline's 29.2x describes the pre-Luminex company; 19x to 20x is my view of a fair multiple for DiaSorin as it is now. Bearing on the case: the fair multiple supports "reversion to normal" in step 5 only if normal is redefined as about 20x, which cuts the reward in step 6 from the guideline's figure to a smaller but still worthwhile one.

The guideline: 29.2x. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for the Broadening phase is 29.2x two-year forward earnings, the 80th percentile of the stock's ten-year history and 81% above today's 16.2x.

My view of the guideline: too high for the business as it now is. The ten-year range (10th percentile 17.4x, median 23.8x, 90th percentile 32.5x) was earned by a different company. From 2016 to 2021 DiaSorin grew revenue at double-digit rates, with a return on capital near 26% and no debt, and the pandemic then pushed the multiple above 40x. Today DiaSorin grows 5% to 6%, earns about 10% on capital, carries 1.8x leverage and faces a contested core. The multiple's history since the Luminex purchase is the better guide: the multiple has been above 24x in none of the last 48 months and above 22x in only a handful.

What I think is fair: 19x to 20x after a period of clean delivery, 17x to 18x now. About 19x to 20x is fair in a period of clean delivery: above the ten-year 10th percentile (17.4x), below the five-year median (20.9x), and consistent with roughly 10% EPS growth, a 33% margin and cash conversion at or above 100%. In the present phase, with forecasts still uncertain, 17x to 18x is fair. bioMérieux at 17.8x, with lower margins but net cash and the stronger molecular position, is a fair cross-check.

Against the market. The sell-side's mean target of about €82 implies roughly today's multiple. I am somewhat more constructive than the sell-side and far less constructive than the guideline.

What would change my view. Evidence that growth can return to 8% or more with rising returns on capital (NES at scale, tuberculosis defended) would justify a multiple in the low 20s. I cannot see what would justify 29x.

Score: 79, set by the Rater. Cheap on one measure and neutral on the other gives B; placed low in the band because much of the cheapness is deserved: the 23.8x ten-year median was earned by a pre-Luminex company growing 11% at a 26% return, the stock has not traded above 24x in 48 months, and the memo's own fair 19-20x is only about 20% above today.

#12 Total shareholder return

Conclusion: the expected return is about +17% probability-weighted over 18 months, and 11% to 17% a year over three years on my multiples, against a mechanical +108% over 18 months and 33% a year over three years at the guideline multiple. Bearing on the case: the return quantifies step 6 and shows that the skew is positive in size (+58% against (18)%) but not in probability.

The starting point: 16.4x forward earnings. On my forecasts, EPS for the twelve months ending 24 months from now is €4.80, so the shares trade on 16.4x that EPS (the Phases data show 16.2x on consensus). The dividend yield is 1.7%, and the free cash flow yield is about 5.2% on a market value of about €3.9bn (49.3m shares; FactSet's €4.3bn uses the pre-buyback share count).

Earnings growth: +14.8% in 18 months, +31% in three years. In 18 months, the same forward EPS measure is €5.51 (seven-twelfths of FY2029 and five-twelfths of FY2030), +14.8%. In three years it is about €6.28 (FY2030 extended by 9%), +31%, or 9.3% a year.

Dividends: 3.4% in 18 months, 5.3% in three years. Two dividends fall within 18 months (€1.33 and €1.38), worth 3.4% of today's price; three fall within three years (adding €1.45), worth 5.3%. I assume no further buyback; the remaining free cash flow repays about €130m of debt a year, which is already counted in EPS growth.

At the guideline fair multiple of 29.2x.

  • 18 months: earnings growth of +14.8% and a multiple +78% higher (16.4x to 29.2x) compound to a price of about €161 (+104%); with 3.4% of dividends, the total return is about +108%.
  • Three years: earnings growth of +31% and the same +78% on the multiple give a price of about €183 (+133%); with 5.3% of dividends, the total return is about +138%, or 33% a year.

My own estimate: about +61% over three years at my fair multiple. I do not expect the multiple leg above to be earned, for the reasons in topic #11. At my fair multiple of 19.5x, the three-year return is +55% in price plus 5.3% in dividends: about +61%, or 17% a year. At an unchanged multiple the three-year return is about +36%, or 11% a year, which is simply earnings growth plus the dividend.

Over 18 months, by case:

What drives the 18-month cases. In the base case, about 15 points come from earnings rolling forward, about 8 from a one-turn rerating (16.4x to 17.5x) as two guidance events pass, and about 3 from dividends. The worse case uses the multiple the market paid at the last scare (12.4x to 12.9x) and lands close to Morgan Stanley's bear-case value of €62. The better case stops at the five-year median multiple.

Against the market and what would change my view. The sell-side's targets imply almost no return; my return is higher because I let the forward earnings roll and allow one turn of rerating. A guidance cut on 12-Mar-27 would move weight from the base case to the worse case; a raised guide during 2027 would move weight to the better case.

End notes

Sources and dates. The latest Earnings Review on file is dated 9-Sep-26 and covers the half-year to June 2026 (reported 31-Jul-26); FactSet's financials end at that same period and show nothing later, but the Change Forces, Leadership and Risks reports carry the third-quarter results of 12-Nov-26, and I use those figures. The four standard reports are dated: Change Forces 24-Nov-26; Business Foundations 2-Sep-26; Leadership Foundations 24-Nov-26; Risks 24-Nov-26.

Charts. Charts in visuals/drawn/ were drawn for this page from the memo's figures: the EPS bridge (topic #5) from the Financial Analyst's model lines, the guidance timeline (topic #4) from the record by year, and the multiple ladder (topic #11) from judgement 5 and topic #11. Charts in visuals/drawn-copy-editor/ were drawn in the copy edit from the memo's own figures: target prices against estimates (topic #8) and the three-year return by exit multiple (topic #12).

Topic #2, NES run time. Some expert comments in the Risks report attach PLEX's two-hour run time to NES; the product descriptions give NES about 15 minutes, so I read the Risks report's attribution as an error.

Topic #3, peer table. Roche is not in the peer table because its financials block could not be built.

Topic #6, the fourth quarter of 2026. The reports disagree on the Molecular growth that a fourth quarter of about +11% requires (one passage says at least 11%, another at least 43%); the memo uses its own arithmetic of 25% to 30%.

Topic #6, the basis of the Financial Analyst's model. The model's FY2023 to FY2025 EBITDA and EPS are FactSet's reported measures, not the company's adjusted basis used elsewhere in this memo: for FY2025, the model shows EBITDA of 432.8 against the adjusted 394, and EPS of 3.71 against the adjusted 4.06. The model's forecasts are on the adjusted basis. The model's FY2026 EPS of 4.10 uses year-end shares, where the memo's 4.01 uses the FY2026 average of about 50.5m. The model's equity free cash flow (130.7 for FY2026, rising to 228.8 for FY2030) is lower than the memo's free cash flow (187 to 266) because the memo's measure is struck before lease payments, as the company and consensus measure it, and assumes cash tax below the profit-and-loss charge.

Topic #9, net debt. The Leadership report states the net debt figures the wrong way round; €782m at 30-Sep-26, up from €580m at end-2025, is correct.

Topic #12, how the model splits the return. The model's split is on the return's own basis: the two-year-forward price-to-earnings multiple and two-year-forward EPS, today against each horizon. The multiple and earnings parts multiply (1 plus one part, times 1 plus the other, less 1, is the share price's change); dividends add to that. The template's own split (TSR Dupont sheet, rows 46 and 47) measures the same return on trailing twelve-month earnings and the trailing multiple: for the 18-month column, +117.4% from the multiple and (9.2)% from earnings; for the three-year column, +112.6% from the multiple and +4.3% from earnings. The template's split reads differently when earnings over the next twelve months are flat or falling, so the model's own split is the one to use. The model's two horizons are its fixed columns after the last reported period, so they end on the dates shown (31-Dec-27 and 30-Jun-29), not 18 months and three years from today.

Figures corrected

None. Every figure the memo states about DiaSorin's past and reported results that the Financial Analyst's model covers agrees with the model on the same basis: FY2025 revenue of 1,195 and growth of +0.8%, last year's revenue growth of 1% in the peer table, and net debt of €580m at end-2025. The model's historical EBITDA (406.7 for FY2024, 432.8 for FY2025) and EPS (3.44 and 3.71) are FactSet's reported measures, which the model's own notes say differ from the company's adjusted basis (EBITDA 394 and EPS 4.06 for FY2025), so the memo's adjusted figures were kept. Figures the model does not cover, such as revenue growth of 11% a year in the decade to 2023 and FY2025 free cash flow of 209, were left as they are.
